title: India's Prediabetes Crisis: 136 Million Adults, Most of Them Unaware
excerpt: With 15.3 per cent of the population in a reversible pre-diabetic state, experts say opportunistic screening — not waiting for symptoms — is the only way to prevent a full-blown epidemic.
body:
• The ICMR-INDIAB study found that 136 million Indians — 15.3 per cent of the adult population — are living with prediabetes, a reversible condition that most are unaware of.
  • Among adults under 40 screened at Indian diagnostic labs, 38 per cent of fasting glucose results were abnormal, pointing to a sharp rise in early-onset metabolic dysfunction.
  • Prediabetes is largely reversible through lifestyle changes including diet modification, physical activity and weight management — but only if caught in time.
  • South Asians in the US face similar risk, with a Northwestern study finding 30 per cent prediabetes prevalence by age 45 among the diaspora.

Mansi Kashyap, a 29-year-old chartered accountant in Delhi, spent two years dismissing her fatigue and changing body shape as side effects of work stress. When excessive thirst and frequent urination finally drove her to a doctor, the diagnosis was prediabetes — a metabolic grey zone she had never heard of.

Her experience, reported by Livemint, is far from unusual. According to the landmark ICMR-INDIAB study conducted by the Indian Council of Medical Research, at least 136 million Indian adults — 15.3 per cent of the population — are living with prediabetes. Most have no idea.

A Silent Epidemic Among the Young

Unlike full-blown Type 2 diabetes, prediabetes rarely announces itself with obvious symptoms. Blood sugar levels are elevated but not yet high enough to meet diagnostic thresholds. The condition is typically discovered incidentally during routine blood work — if screening happens at all.

"In India, nearly 50 per cent of people living with diabetes are unaware of their condition, and prediabetes often goes unnoticed until it progresses," said Aditya Kandoi, CEO of Redcliffe Labs. "Routine screenings often miss prediabetes in younger or asymptomatic individuals because they aren't perceived as 'at risk.'"

Data from Mahajan Imaging and Labs underscores the scale of the problem among India's younger population. Among adults under 40 screened for metabolic markers, nearly 38 per cent of fasting glucose results, 20 per cent of HbA1c readings, and 35 per cent of post-prandial glucose results came back abnormal.

"The prediabetic stage is crucial because it represents a window of opportunity: blood sugar levels are elevated but not yet high enough to be classified as diabetes."

— Dr Paras Agarwal, Marengo Asia Hospitals

Beyond Diet: Stress and Sleep as Metabolic Triggers

Experts increasingly point to factors beyond diet and exercise as drivers of India's prediabetes surge. Chronic stress, poor sleep and irregular meal timing are emerging as independent risk factors for metabolic dysfunction.

"In urban settings, we increasingly see young Indians with borderline or elevated fasting insulin scores, despite normal body weight and diet," said Dr Jaspreet Singh, an endocrinologist at Ujala Cygnus Group of Hospitals. "Sleeping for less than six hours, high nighttime smartphone usage, and work-related stress are playing a clinically significant role in early onset metabolic dysfunction."

Dr Aarathi Bellary of KIMS Hospitals in Hyderabad describes a "wired but tired" phenotype common in urban India: people who exercise occasionally and avoid obvious junk food but compensate with poor sleep and high stress, tipping into prediabetes despite a normal BMI. She also flagged a growing issue in semi-urban areas: widespread consumption of carbonated, high-sugar drinks with virtually no awareness of the metabolic consequences.

Reversible — But Only With Early Action

The critical distinction between prediabetes and diabetes is reversibility. "Unlike diabetes, which is considered remissible at best, prediabetes is largely reversible," said Dr Agarwal. Improving dietary patterns, increasing physical activity and managing weight can reduce insulin resistance and, in many cases, return blood sugar to normal levels — delaying or preventing diabetes onset by years.

Yet India's healthcare system remains largely reactive. "Most interventions begin only after a confirmed diabetes diagnosis, rather than during the warning stage," noted Dr Singh. He called for integrating community-based HbA1c testing into primary health centres and corporate wellness programmes — a shift from identifying disease to intercepting it.

A Diaspora Concern Too

The metabolic vulnerabilities driving India's prediabetes numbers do not stay at the border. South Asians in the United States develop insulin resistance and cardiovascular risk at lower BMI thresholds than other ethnic groups. A major study from Northwestern University found that 30 per cent of South Asian American adults had prediabetes by age 45, despite reporting among the healthiest dietary patterns of any group studied.

Padma Bhushan Dr Ambrish Mithal, chair of Endocrinology and Diabetes at Max Healthcare, called for annual screening for everyone aged 25 and above. "The challenge now is to transition from identifying disease to intercepting it — to make metabolic screening and risk-profiling a routine part of health checks for young adults, not just middle-aged adults," he said.

For the 136 million Indians and millions more in the diaspora living in this metabolic grey zone, the window for action is open — but it will not stay open indefinitely.

The genetic and metabolic factors driving India's prediabetes crisis travel with the diaspora, making awareness and screening equally urgent for NRIs.
